title_en: Homes or parkland? Building on urban green space
title_he: דיור או פארק? בנייה על שטחים ירוקים בעיר
prompt: Argue whether cities facing housing shortages should build homes on part of their urban parkland, using the fictional case of Halvarden, and respond to opposing views.

instructions.en: Write an analytical argumentative essay of 800-1000 words. The three sources in the source pack are illustrative: the city, the park, the organisations, the columnist and every figure were invented for this task and describe nothing in the real world. Before you take a position, evaluate the sources: what kind of source is each, what does it establish, and what are its limits? The opinion column mixes a genuine point with weak reasoning. Identify at least two reasoning flaws in it (for example, an unsupported chain of consequences, a false choice, or an attack on people rather than their arguments), explain why each is weak, and say what its strongest legitimate point is; naming a fallacy is optional, explaining the weakness is not. Then argue your own position on the general question, apply it to the Halvarden case, cite the sources by author and year (e.g. Halvarden City Planning Office, 2025), and respond to the strongest opposing view. Finally, audit your own draft for the weaknesses you found in the column: sweeping words such as "all", "never" and "everyone", unfair descriptions of the other side, and claims stronger than your evidence. Score your draft against the rubric yourself before you revise it.

required_elements: a precise thesis on building on urban parkland, applied to the Halvarden case
an evaluation of all three sources: what each establishes and its main limitation
at least two reasoning flaws in the opinion column identified, explained and answered
acknowledgement of the column's strongest legitimate point
author-year citation for every source-derived idea
the strongest opposing view stated fairly and rebutted with reasoning or evidence
a conclusion that adds no new arguments

checklist.en: Claim: my thesis takes a precise position on building on urban parkland and applies it to the Halvarden case, with any conditions stated.
Reasons: each reason supports my thesis directly, and I have checked my own reasoning for unsupported chains of consequences, false choices and overgeneralisations.
Evidence: I cite each source by author and year, say what it can and cannot show, and explain at least two weaknesses in the column's reasoning.
Counterargument: I state the strongest opposing view fairly, including the column's best point, without caricaturing it or its author.
Rebuttal: my response rests on reasoning or evidence, not on attacking the people who disagree, and my thesis changes if I concede a point.
Conclusion: my conclusion restates the refined thesis and adds no new arguments.

scaffold.en: Read each source and note who produced it, for what purpose, what it claims, and what it does not show.
Map the column's argument: list its premises and its conclusion. Mark each step that is unsupported, unfair or a false choice, and write a one-line fix or answer next to it.
Decide your thesis, then argue against your own conclusion: write the best paragraph the other side could write.
Plan by idea, not by source, and decide where each source supports, qualifies or challenges a point.
Bias audit of your draft: circle every "all", "never" and "everyone" and every description of your opponents; qualify or correct where needed.

source_pack.title: Source A · City report (fictional): Halvarden City Planning Office (2025), "Housing and Open Space Review", summary
source_pack.text:
Halvarden's population has grown faster than its housing supply for ten years, and average rents have risen faster than average incomes over the same period.
The review examines building on the northern edge of Orrin Fields, about 15% of the park's area. This part is currently mown grass and a surface car park. The office estimates that it could provide about 900 homes, 40% of them at rents below the market rate. The rest of the park, including the lake, the woodland and the sports pitches, would be protected from future building by a legal designation.
The review compares three alternatives: converting empty office buildings (an estimated 300 to 500 homes, more slowly and at a higher cost per home); building higher on existing housing estates; and building at the edge of the city, which would increase commuting by car.
The office describes its cost estimates as "preliminary" and notes that no independent environmental assessment of the northern edge has yet been carried out.

source_pack.title: Source B · Opinion column (fictional): Dana Merrow (2025), "Hands off our park", Halvarden Evening Courier
source_pack.text:
The planners say they want only "a corner" of Orrin Fields. Don't believe it. Once the first block goes up, the next corner will follow, and in twenty years our grandchildren will have no park at all.
The choice is simple: either we protect our green spaces, or we accept that Halvarden becomes a concrete jungle. It is also worth asking where the authors of this review live. I would bet that most of them go home to houses with large private gardens. Everyone I have spoken to on my street is against the plan.
And the "mown grass" that the review dismisses is not empty. It is where children from the flats on Wren Street play football every evening, and where older residents walk because it is the only flat, open ground within reach. Once a park is built on, it is gone for good; a housing shortage, however serious, can be solved in other ways.

source_pack.title: Source C · Survey summary (fictional): Halvarden Residents' Panel (2025), "Views on Orrin Fields"
source_pack.text:
An online questionnaire was posted on the city council's website for three weeks and answered by 1,240 residents who chose to respond.
58% opposed building on any part of Orrin Fields, 34% supported building there if most of the homes were affordable, and 8% were unsure. Support was higher among respondents aged 18 to 34 and among people who rent their homes.
The panel notes that respondents selected themselves, and that homeowners aged over 55 made up a larger share of respondents than of the city's adult population.

exemplar.outline:
Parallel prompt (not your question; read this only after you have written your own essay): Argue whether the fictional town of Rensby should convert its central multi-storey car park into a public square, and respond to opposing views. The exemplar draws on three fictional sources: a council proposal (Rensby Town Council, 2024), a traffic survey (Ostrander, 2024) and an opinion column (Calloway, 2024).

Thesis: Rensby should convert the car park into a public square, on condition that accessible parking is kept within a short walk of the main street, because the town centre needs public space more than it needs this particular car park, and the strongest objection can be met.

I. Introduction: the proposal; what is at stake; thesis.
II. Evaluating the sources: what the council proposal establishes and leaves out; the survey's sample (weekday mornings only); the column's mix of a legitimate concern and weak reasoning.
III. Argument 1: the car park is often half empty outside peak hours (Ostrander, 2024), so the land is underused; qualified, because the survey covered weekdays only.
IV. Argument 2: a square would serve groups who currently have nowhere to meet in the centre.
V. Argument 3: a square makes the centre a place to stay, not only to pass through.
VI. Strongest objection and rebuttal (annotated below): the column's unsupported chain of consequences and personal attack answered; its accessibility point conceded and built into the thesis.
VII. Conclusion: the refined thesis; the further evidence that would settle the remaining doubt (weekend parking data).
exemplar.annotated_paragraph:
From the exemplar essay on the parallel prompt above (section VI: objection and rebuttal; all sources are fictional)

[1] The strongest case against the square comes from Calloway's (2024) opinion column, but it needs to be separated from the weaker reasoning that surrounds it. [2] Calloway claims that closing the car park is "the first step towards banning cars from the town altogether", yet the column offers no evidence that further closures are planned, and the council's proposal concerns a single site (Rensby Town Council, 2024). [3] Similarly, the suggestion that the plan's supporters "never shop in the town centre" attacks the people rather than their reasons. [4] Beneath these weaknesses, however, lies a legitimate concern: residents with limited mobility depend on parking close to the shops, and the proposal says little about where they would park. [5] This point does not defeat the case for a square, but it does refine it: the conversion should go ahead only if accessible parking spaces are kept within a short walk of the main street.

Notes
[1] Engages the source's strongest version instead of a straw man, and signals that the source will be evaluated, not simply cited.
[2] Spot and fix: identifies an unsupported chain of consequences and answers it with evidence from a second source.
[3] Explains the second flaw by what it does (it attacks people, not reasons). The label "ad hominem" is optional; the explanation is not.
[4] Concession: credits the legitimate point, which shows that the evaluation is not one-sided.
[5] The concession changes the thesis (a condition is added), so the counterargument is integrated rather than dismissed.
